neighbors.heading: don't send them back
neighbors.text: Today Thoreau walked a man who had escaped slavery to the train, and raged when Boston sent another back. The Torah gives a law for that very moment: "Thou shalt not deliver unto his master a bondman that is escaped from his master unto thee." The next verse says he may live wherever he chooses among you, and no one may wrong him.
neighbors.difference: Thoreau acted on his own conscience, against the law of his state. In the Torah, sheltering the one who fled is itself the law, a commandment Jews read as given by God.
neighbors.shared: the one running from chains is owed a door, not a return.
neighbors.sources: Deuteronomy 23:16-17 (JPS 1917; 23:15-16 in many Bibles; v. 17 paraphrased)

neighbors.heading: not a trade in people
neighbors.text: Today Thoreau would not make peace with a state that sent people back into slavery. The Buddha drew a line in daily work. He told lay followers there are five trades they should not take up, and one of them is trading in human beings. A living, in his teaching, should never be made from selling a person.
neighbors.difference: Thoreau's stand was public, aimed at a whole state and its law. The Buddha's teaching is about your own livelihood, part of the path's right livelihood, and it binds by choice, not by law.
neighbors.shared: no living is worth making out of another person's freedom.

neighbors.heading: the race for more
neighbors.text: Today Thoreau worried that people spend their whole lives getting a living, and never get around to living. A short surah of the Qur'an says it plainly: "Rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you until ye come to the graves." Many Muslims read it as a wake-up call: the race for more can fill a lifetime before anyone asks what it was for.
neighbors.difference: Thoreau asks what in your days money couldn't buy, and answers with walks and friendship. The surah ends by saying people will be asked about the pleasures they were given, an answer owed to God.
neighbors.shared: a life is more than what it earns.

neighbors.heading: keep your horses
neighbors.text: Today Thoreau asked what in your life is more than a living. In the Katha Upanishad, Death offers the boy Nachiketa wealth, long life, horses and music. Nachiketa turns it all down. Keep your horses, he says, in paraphrase; no one is ever satisfied by wealth. He wants to know what lasts.
neighbors.difference: Thoreau's answer is close to home: a walk, a friend, a song. Nachiketa's question is about the self that is not born and does not die, and he learns it from Death as his teacher.
neighbors.shared: asking what lasts is worth more than any prize.

neighbors.heading: remember, and remember again
neighbors.text: Today William James said the root of character is bringing a wandering attention back, over and over. Sikhs know that return well. The Sukhmani Sahib opens: simro simar simar sukh pavo. In paraphrase: remember, remember, keep remembering God, and find peace. Simran is coming back to the Name, again and again, through an ordinary day.
neighbors.difference: James describes a power of the mind that builds will and judgment. For Sikhs, the return is to Waheguru, the Name of God, and the peace it brings is a gift of grace, not only of effort.
neighbors.shared: wandering off is human; coming back is the practice.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262 (Sukhmani Sahib, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: martha, martha
neighbors.text: Today William James prized the mind that comes back after it drifts. In Luke's Gospel, Martha is busy and pulled every which way while her sister Mary sits listening. Jesus calls her back by name, twice: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful."
neighbors.difference: James wants attention returned to whatever you choose. In the Gospel, Mary chose to sit at Jesus' feet and hear his word, and many Christians read the one needful thing as listening to him.
neighbors.shared: being called back gently is a kindness, not a scolding.

neighbors.heading: don't chase the past
neighbors.text: Today a study showed part of the mind staying behind on the last task. A Buddhist discourse names that trailing mind. In paraphrase: don't chase after the past or pin your hopes on the future; the past is gone, the future not yet come. See clearly what is here now, and do today what needs doing.
neighbors.difference: Leroy's fix is practical: finish a task, or write down where you'll pick it up. The Buddha's teaching aims further, at seeing each moment arise and pass, as part of the path to freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: the room you're in is the one that needs you.

neighbors.heading: sufficient for the day
neighbors.text: Today the mind kept trailing behind, still in the last room. Jesus speaks to the other direction, the mind running ahead: "Be not therefore solicitous for to morrow; for the morrow will be solicitous for itself. Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof." Catholics hear it inside a larger trust: God feeds the birds and clothes the lilies.
neighbors.difference: The research is about the leftovers of one task. Jesus speaks of worry, and his answer is trust in a Father who knows what you need, something no study measures.
neighbors.shared: one day at a time is enough to carry.

neighbors.heading: the offering is the meal
neighbors.text: Today a meal became a short meditation. Some Hindus pause before eating to recite a verse of the Bhagavad Gita. In paraphrase: the offering is Brahman, the food offered is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman; whoever sees Brahman in the act goes to Brahman. The plate becomes an altar, and eating becomes worship.
neighbors.difference: The research asks you to slow down and notice fullness. The verse asks you to see the whole meal, food, eater and fire, as Brahman, the one reality, and to eat as an offering.
neighbors.shared: a pause before eating turns food into a gift.

neighbors.heading: eat, be satisfied, bless
neighbors.text: Today the lesson asked you to notice when you're full. The Torah ties fullness to thanks: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." Jewish practice has blessings before eating, and from this verse comes the grace after meals, said once the meal is done.
neighbors.difference: Mindful eating listens to the body's signal. In Jewish practice the blessing is a commandment, words of thanks to God, said whether or not the meal was eaten slowly.
neighbors.shared: noticing you're full is the first step to saying thank you.

neighbors.heading: as he did aforetime
neighbors.text: Today a plan with a when turned a hope into a habit. Daniel had one. When a law forbade it, he went home, "and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime." Same window, same times, same as before.
neighbors.difference: Gollwitzer's plans help people reach goals they set. Daniel's set times are faithfulness to God, kept even when it was dangerous, and Christians read the story as trust, not technique.
neighbors.shared: a set time can hold you when your will is shaky.

neighbors.heading: prayer at fixed hours
neighbors.text: Today the lesson hung a practice on a when. The Qur'an builds the whole day that way: "Lo! worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." Five daily prayers, each with its own window of time, called by the adhan. The when is already there. Muslims answer it.
neighbors.difference: An implementation intention is a plan you choose for a goal you choose. For Muslims, the prayer times are given by God, and keeping them is worship, not a habit trick.
neighbors.shared: a set time makes room for what matters most.

neighbors.heading: the left hand doesn't know
neighbors.text: Today a promised prize made drawing feel like work. Jesus teaches giving without an audience: "But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth. That thy alms may be in secret." Catholics read it as doing good for God and for the person in front of you, not for praise.
neighbors.difference: The study warns against outside rewards. Jesus goes on, "and thy Father who seeth in secret will repay thee": not no reward, but a hidden one, from God rather than from people watching.
neighbors.shared: goodness grows best when no one's keeping score.

neighbors.heading: service without wanting
neighbors.text: Today the children who drew for a prize stopped drawing for joy. Sikhs have a name for the other way: nishkam seva, service without wanting anything back. In the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan writes, in paraphrase, that one who serves without desire for reward reaches the Lord. The ladle in the langar isn't lifted for a certificate.
neighbors.difference: The study is about keeping your own interest alive. For Sikhs, selfless service loosens haumai, the ego, and its aim is nearness to Waheguru, not a happier hobby.
neighbors.shared: help given freely keeps its joy.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286 (Sukhmani Sahib, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seven times, and up
neighbors.text: Today kindness after a failure helped people try again. Proverbs puts it in one line: "For a righteous man falleth seven times, and riseth up again." The righteous one isn't someone who never falls. It's someone who keeps getting up. Jewish tradition gives that rising a name: teshuvah, returning.
neighbors.difference: Self-compassion is kindness you give yourself. In Judaism, teshuvah turns toward God and toward anyone you've hurt, with regret, repair and a changed path.
neighbors.shared: falling isn't the end of the story; getting up is part of it.

neighbors.heading: the moon out of the clouds
neighbors.text: Today gentleness after a lapse turned out to help, not excuse. The Dhammapada says: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." The old mistake doesn't define him. The turning does.
neighbors.difference: The studies measure motivation after one failure. The Dhammapada speaks of a whole life turning, and in Buddhist teaching what clears the clouds is a person's own practice, not forgiveness from a God.
neighbors.shared: the past doesn't get the last word on who you are.

neighbors.heading: mercy, passed on
neighbors.text: Today Mencius said compassion begins like a spring just starting to flow. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ taught that mercy is something you practice and pass along. In paraphrase: the merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful; be merciful to those on earth, and the One in heaven will be merciful to you.
neighbors.difference: Mencius finds a seed of goodness in every heart, grown by human effort. In Islam, mercy begins with God, Ar-Rahman, and human mercy is an answer to His.
neighbors.shared: mercy grows when you give it away.

neighbors.heading: friendliness, on purpose
neighbors.text: Today compassion turned out to be something a class could grow. Patanjali's Yoga Sutras treat it as practice too. In paraphrase: cultivate friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward those who suffer, gladness toward the good, and calm toward those who do wrong, and the mind grows clear and settled.
neighbors.difference: Mencius grows compassion to make a good person and a good society. Patanjali names it as one way to a still mind, a step toward the seer resting in its own nature.
neighbors.shared: a kind heart can be practiced, one person at a time.

neighbors.heading: earn, and share
neighbors.text: Today money spent on someone else came back as a happier evening. Guru Nanak said it simply. In paraphrase: one who eats what they earn by honest work, and gives some of it away with their own hands, knows the path. Some Sikhs set aside a tenth for others and call it dasvandh.
neighbors.difference: The study measured a mood at the end of a day. For Sikhs, sharing, vand chhakna, is part of a life lived in remembrance of God, beside honest work and the Name.
neighbors.shared: what you share with your hands comes back to your heart.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245 (Sarang ki Var, Salok Mahalla 1, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a cheerful giver
neighbors.text: Today a little money, spent for someone else, made people glad. Paul writes to a church collecting for the poor: "Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." Not how much. How gladly.
neighbors.difference: The researchers found giving can make the giver happier. Paul points the gladness toward God, who loves the cheerful giver, and Christians give in thanks for what they believe God first gave them.
neighbors.shared: a gift given gladly blesses both hands.

neighbors.heading: as a mother
neighbors.text: Today Hierocles drew circles and asked his readers to pull the far ones closer. The Buddha's discourse on loving-kindness widens the same way. In paraphrase: as a mother would guard her only child with her life, so let one grow a boundless heart toward all beings, above, below and all around, without hatred or ill will.
neighbors.difference: Hierocles and Singer reason the circle wider. The Buddha's way is practice: loving-kindness grown in meditation, until no line is left between near and far.
neighbors.shared: the circle of care can keep getting bigger.

neighbors.heading: even the enemy
neighbors.text: Today the circle kept widening, from family out to strangers. Jesus draws it to the hardest ring of all: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you." The reason he gives: the Father makes his sun rise on the good and the bad.
neighbors.difference: Singer argues that reason pushes concern outward. Catholics hear a command of Christ, and see the strength to keep it as God's grace, so people may become children of their Father in heaven.
neighbors.shared: even the hardest person is still inside the circle.

neighbors.heading: first, how you treat others
neighbors.text: Today a critic asked what calm is for, if it floats free of goodness. Patanjali's yoga answers with an order. Its eight limbs begin with the yamas: non-harm, truthfulness, not stealing, restraint, not grasping. Posture and breath come after. In paraphrase, he calls these a great vow for everyone, not bound by birth, place, time or circumstance.
neighbors.difference: The Dhammapada's order belongs to the Buddha's eightfold path. Patanjali's limbs lead toward the seer resting in its own nature, inside yoga's own frame, not the Buddha's.
neighbors.shared: calm grows best in a life that's kind.

neighbors.heading: deeds before wisdom
neighbors.text: Today a Buddhist verse put not harming before purifying the mind. A rabbi in the Mishnah set a similar order. In paraphrase, Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa said: whoever's fear of sin comes before their wisdom, their wisdom will last; whoever's wisdom comes before their fear of sin, their wisdom won't.
neighbors.difference: The Buddhist order rests on the eightfold path, with no creator God at its center. For the rabbis, fear of sin means awe before God, and good deeds are commandments given in the Torah.
neighbors.shared: knowing more only helps when it makes you kinder.

neighbors.heading: they sang, then went out
neighbors.text: Today the singing classes bonded fastest. On his last night, after supper with his friends, Jesus sang too. Matthew says: "And when they had sung an hymn, they went out into the mount of Olives." A hard night was ahead. They walked into it having sung together first.
neighbors.difference: The study measured how fast classmates felt close. For Christians, singing together is worship, and the closeness that matters most is with God and with the church as one body.
neighbors.shared: voices together can carry what one voice can't.

neighbors.heading: one amin
neighbors.text: Today voices together drew strangers close. In Muslim prayer, after the imam recites the Fatiha, the rows answer: amin. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ taught, in paraphrase, that when the imam says amin, you say amin too, and whoever's amin meets the angels' amin is forgiven.
neighbors.difference: The classes sang songs. Muslims don't count reciting the Qur'an as singing, and they differ among themselves about music. The shared amin is worship, said to God, with the angels joining in.
neighbors.shared: your voice belongs in the chorus, however it sounds.

neighbors.heading: all ye works of the lord
neighbors.text: Today a survey found that time outside goes with feeling well. In the book of Daniel, three young men in a furnace call all creation to praise: "All ye works of the Lord, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him above all for ever." Sun and moon, rain and mountains, birds and beasts, each called by name. The Church still prays it at morning prayer on Sundays and feasts.
neighbors.difference: The study counts minutes for health. The canticle isn't about what nature does for people: it hears creation itself praising its Creator, and joins in.
neighbors.shared: stepping outside can open your eyes to wonder.
neighbors.sources: Daniel 3:57 (Douay-Rheims; the Canticle of the Three Children)

neighbors.heading: where you dwell
neighbors.text: Today two hours outside a week turned out to matter. Guru Nanak sings of the outdoors with wonder. In paraphrase, from the Asa di Var: I am a sacrifice to Your creation, kudrat, where You dwell; Your limits cannot be known. For Sikhs, the woods and fields aren't empty. The Creator is present in them.
neighbors.difference: The survey looks at health and leaves the meaning to you. For Sikhs, nature is where Waheguru dwells, though God is also beyond all creation, never simply the same as it.
neighbors.shared: a walk outside can be a walk with wonder.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469 (Asa di Var, Salok Mahalla 1, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: happy with your portion
neighbors.text: Today lottery winners turned out no happier than their neighbors. Ben Zoma asked in the Mishnah, in paraphrase: who is rich? The one who is happy with their portion. Riches, on this reading, don't sit in a bank. They live in eyes that still see what they already have.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus guarded against taking things for granted by remembering they end. The Jewish way leans on thanks: a portion is received from God, and blessings through the day keep it in view.
neighbors.shared: seeing what you already have is its own kind of wealth.

neighbors.heading: the eight winds
neighbors.text: Today people turned out to adapt, to good fortune and to loss. The Buddha named eight conditions that come to every life: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. In paraphrase, he said they come to the wise and the unwise alike; the wise see them as passing, and aren't swept away.
neighbors.difference: The psychologists describe a pull back to where people started, often unnoticed. The Buddha teaches seeing impermanence on purpose, aiming at a mind free from clinging, not just a steady mood.
neighbors.shared: good days and hard days both pass; you can stay steady.

neighbors.heading: the work of his hands
neighbors.text: Today Baizhang said a day without work is a day without food. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said something near it. In paraphrase: no one has eaten better food than what they earned by the work of their own hands, and the prophet David used to eat from the work of his own hands.
neighbors.difference: In Zen, work is practice toward awakening, a pan washed as you'd sit on the cushion. In Islam, honest work done with a right intention is worship of God, and earning your own bread is part of it.
neighbors.shared: ordinary work, done well, can be holy ground.

neighbors.heading: skill in action
neighbors.text: Today a Zen cook dried mushrooms in the heat and called it practice. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna not to step away from work: even keeping the body alive needs action. And, in paraphrase: yoga is skill in action. Work done without clinging to its fruits becomes the path itself.
neighbors.difference: Zen work trains attention in the moment, without a creator at its center. Krishna asks that work be done as an offering to him, the Lord, so each task becomes devotion as well as discipline.
neighbors.shared: the task in your hands can be your practice.

neighbors.heading: this is your chance
neighbors.text: Today a blind turtle and a floating yoke showed how rare a human life is. Sikhs hear a hymn about the same opening in Rehras, the evening prayer. In paraphrase: you have been given this human body; this is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe. Other work won't help; join the company of the holy and remember the Name.
neighbors.difference: Lamrim teachers point to a rare birth so it can be used for awakening, with no creator at the center. For Sikhs, the chance is to meet Waheguru, by grace and by remembering the Name.
neighbors.shared: this life is a rare opening; today is worth using.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12 (Rehras, Asa Mahalla 5, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: number our days
neighbors.text: Today the lesson called this life an unlikely opening, worth using now. A psalm asks for help seeing it: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." Counting the days isn't meant to frighten. It's meant to wake a heart up to the ones it has.
neighbors.difference: In Buddhist teaching, a human birth is rare among many lives. In the Christian telling, a person lives one life on earth, made and loved by God, and the psalm turns counting into a prayer.
neighbors.shared: counting your days can make each one count.

neighbors.heading: the name, over and over
neighbors.text: Today a pilgrim walked across Russia saying one short prayer until it seemed to pray itself. Pure Land Buddhists in Japan keep a practice with the same shape: the nembutsu, Namu Amida Butsu, I take refuge in Amida Buddha, said again and again. The teacher Honen put it simply, in paraphrase: just say the name, with trust.
neighbors.difference: The pilgrim calls on Jesus Christ, Son of God, for mercy. Pure Land Buddhists call on Amida, trusting his vow to bring them to his Pure Land: a Buddha, not a creator God.
neighbors.shared: a short line, said with your whole heart, can walk with you all day.

neighbors.heading: your longing is your prayer
neighbors.text: Today a pilgrim asked how anyone could pray without ceasing. Saint Augustine gave his own answer. In paraphrase, from his sermons on the Psalms: your longing is your prayer; if your longing never stops, your prayer never stops. Prayer can run under everything, as a heart kept turned toward God.
neighbors.difference: The pilgrim keeps the Jesus Prayer, an Orthodox practice counted on a prayer rope. Augustine, a saint Catholics and Orthodox both honor, places unceasing prayer in desire itself, with or without words.
neighbors.shared: a quiet longing can be a prayer all day long.
neighbors.sources: Augustine, Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm 38 (37 in the Douay numbering) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the lord in every heart
neighbors.text: Today George Fox asked Friends to answer "that of God in every one." In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says something close. In paraphrase: the Lord dwells in the hearts of all beings. And: one who sees me everywhere, and everything in me, is never lost to me. The greeting namaste is often explained as a bow to that presence.
neighbors.difference: For Quakers, the light in each person is of God, not the person being God. Some Hindu schools, like Advaita Vedanta, go further: the deepest self is not other than Brahman. Others keep God and soul distinct.
neighbors.shared: every person you meet is worth answering with care.

neighbors.heading: silence is praise
neighbors.text: Today Friends sat in silence, waiting together. A psalm, in the Jewish translation, says: "For Thee silence is praise, O God, in Zion." And when God passes by the prophet Elijah, God isn't in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in "a still small voice." Sometimes the holy comes quietly.
neighbors.difference: Quaker worship can be almost all silence, with words only when someone is moved. Jewish prayer is mostly set words, said in community, with silence held inside it, as in the Amidah, prayed softly.
neighbors.shared: a shared silence can say more than a speech.

neighbors.heading: in every thing
neighbors.text: Today a day filled up with blessings, a hundred small doors. Paul asks a young church for the same habit, in one line: "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you." Christians who say grace before a meal keep a small piece of it at every table.
neighbors.difference: Jewish blessings have set words for each thing, opening with "blessed are you." Paul's call is open: thanks in every circumstance, in any words, offered to God through Christ.
neighbors.shared: a thank-you can turn an ordinary thing back into a gift.

neighbors.heading: bismillah, alhamdulillah
neighbors.text: Today blessings turned ordinary things into small doors. Muslims carry short words for the same moments. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ taught, in paraphrase, to say bismillah, in the name of God, before eating, and alhamdulillah, praise be to God, after a sneeze. The day fills with small reminders that everything comes from God.
neighbors.difference: Jewish berachot open with "blessed are you" and name the thing at hand. The Muslim phrases name God first, and saying them is itself remembrance, dhikr, which Muslims hold God rewards.
neighbors.shared: small words can make a whole day feel like a gift.

neighbors.heading: god among the pots and pans
neighbors.text: Today a Sufi saying kept the hand at work and the heart with the Friend. Brother Lawrence, a Carmelite lay brother, worked in a monastery kitchen. In paraphrase, he said his time of work was no different from his time of prayer: in the clatter of the kitchen, with several people calling at once, he held God as calmly as on his knees.
neighbors.difference: The Naqshbandi way repeats God's name silently in the heart. Brother Lawrence describes a simple, loving attention to God's presence, the calm he knew kneeling before the Blessed Sacrament, which Catholics hold is Christ himself.
neighbors.shared: the busiest room can still have a quiet center.
neighbors.sources: Brother Lawrence, The Practice of the Presence of God, Fourth Conversation (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: hands at work, mind with god
neighbors.text: Today Sufis kept the heart with God while the hands kept working. Kabir, whose verses sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, puts it in one salok. In paraphrase: with your hands and feet, do all your work; keep your mind with the Pure One. Sikhs live it as kirat karo and naam japo: honest work, and the Name.
neighbors.difference: Naqshbandi remembrance is passed on through a Sufi order and its masters. Sikhs keep remembrance as householders, guided by the Guru Granth Sahib as their Guru, in the sangat and at work.
neighbors.shared: busy hands and a quiet heart can share one day.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1376 (Salok Kabir, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: like a weaned child
neighbors.text: Today the Yoga Sutras pictured a lake going still. A psalm has its own picture of a quiet soul: "Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul; like a weaned child with his mother; my soul is with me like a weaned child." Not a baby crying for milk. A child resting against a parent, wanting nothing.
neighbors.difference: Patanjali's stilling comes by practice and letting go, so the seer can rest in itself. The psalmist's quiet is trust: the next verse turns to "hope in the LORD," a calm that rests on God.
neighbors.shared: a quiet mind is a resting place, not an empty one.

neighbors.heading: straight as an arrow
neighbors.text: Today yoga was the stilling of the mind's movements. The Dhammapada calls the mind hard to hold, and gives it a craftsman's picture: "As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back."
neighbors.difference: Patanjali speaks of a seer that rests in its own nature once the mind is still. The Buddha teaches calming and seeing the mind without positing a lasting self behind it.
neighbors.shared: a restless mind can be steadied, with patience.

neighbors.heading: the perfume seller
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs said the company you keep changes you. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave a picture for it. In paraphrase: a good companion is like someone who sells musk; even if you buy nothing, you leave smelling sweet. A bad companion is like a blacksmith's bellows; even if no spark touches you, you leave smelling of smoke.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, holy company leads to the Name of God, and the sangat is a body everyone can join. The hadith is practical counsel about everyday friends, part of how a Muslim guards their faith.
neighbors.shared: good friends leave something sweet on you.

neighbors.heading: satsang
neighbors.text: Today the sangat showed how company shapes a person. Hindus use a close word, satsang, the company of truth. A hymn traditionally credited to Shankara climbs a staircase from it. In paraphrase: from good company comes letting go; from letting go, freedom from delusion; from that, a steady truth; and from that, freedom in this very life.
neighbors.difference: Sikh sangat gathers around the Guru Granth Sahib and the Name of Waheguru. In Shankara's verse, good company is the first step toward liberation, the self set free while still living.
neighbors.shared: the people around you can lift you higher.
neighbors.sources: Bhaja Govindam, verse 9, attributed to Adi Shankara (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: conquer the mind
neighbors.text: Today the Great Learning traced peace in the world back to the self. Guru Nanak says it in four words in the Japji, a morning prayer: man jeetai jag jeet. Conquer your mind, and you conquer the world. On this reading, the struggle that matters most starts inside.
neighbors.difference: The Great Learning roots order in study, sincere thought and family duty. For Guru Nanak, the mind is won by living in God's will, hukam, and remembering the Name, not by effort alone.
neighbors.shared: the world gets kinder one tended heart at a time.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6 (Japji Sahib, pauri 28; translation paraphrased)

neighbors.heading: the beam first
neighbors.text: Today the Great Learning said setting the world right starts with tending yourself. Jesus puts it with a carpenter's picture: "Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye." Your own eye first. Then you can help.
neighbors.difference: The Great Learning sees the self as the root of a well-ordered family and state. Jesus speaks of judging others, and Christians see the change in the heart as God's grace at work, not discipline alone.
neighbors.shared: changing the world starts closest to home.

neighbors.heading: little by little
neighbors.text: Today science said attention, habit and compassion grow modestly, like muscles. The Dhammapada says the same of a person: "Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver, one by one, little by little, and from time to time." No sudden fix. Silver gets bright slowly.
neighbors.difference: Science measures small changes and stays modest about what they mean. The Dhammapada's slow work aims at nirvana, a whole freedom from craving, which no study claims to measure.
neighbors.shared: small, steady steps really do add up.

neighbors.heading: faithful in little
neighbors.text: Today the year's science came down to one word: modestly. Jesus praised small faithfulness: "He that is faithful in that which is least, is faithful also in that which is greater." Saint Thérèse of Lisieux built her little way on that spirit: small acts of love, done often, offered to God.
neighbors.difference: The research counts gains made by practice. Thérèse saw her littleness as the point: she trusted God to lift her, like a child carried, rather than climbing by her own strength.
neighbors.shared: the small thing done today is never too small.
neighbors.sources: Luke 16:10 (Douay-Rheims) · Thérèse of Lisieux, Story of a Soul (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: your own dharma
neighbors.text: Today the lesson said "not for me" is a sentence about me, not about the practice. The Bhagavad Gita has a line in that spirit. In paraphrase: better your own dharma, done imperfectly, than another's done well. Krishna tells Arjuna to walk the path that is truly his.
neighbors.difference: The lesson is about letting a practice go kindly. In the Gita, svadharma is the duty that comes with one's nature and place in life, and Krishna is urging Arjuna not to walk away from his.
neighbors.shared: your own path, walked honestly, is the one that fits.

neighbors.heading: why weren't you zusya?
neighbors.text: Today the lesson let some practices go without a sneer. A Hasidic story makes room for being yourself. Rabbi Zusya, near death, was afraid. In paraphrase, he said: in the world to come they won't ask me, why weren't you Moses? They'll ask me, why weren't you Zusya?
neighbors.difference: The lesson sorts practices to find what fits. Zusya's worry is about answering to God for the person he was made to be, inside Jewish life and its commandments.
neighbors.shared: you're only asked to be fully yourself.
neighbors.sources: Hasidic tale of Rabbi Zusya of Hanipol (paraphrase)
